title: Spaced Repetition: Study Less, Remember More

guide.intro: Spaced repetition beats cramming by reviewing material at expanding intervals, so you remember more while studying less.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Cramming feels productive, but much of it is forgotten within days. Spaced repetition reviews material at expanding gaps: 1 day, then 3 days, then 7 days, then 30 days. Each review happens just as the memory starts to fade, which strengthens it.

sections.title: How to use it
sections.text: Test yourself through active recall instead of re-reading notes. Turn each topic into questions or flashcards and answer from memory. Anki is named in the post as a free tool with built-in spaced repetition scheduling.

sections.title: What to watch out for
sections.text: Re-reading alone does not create the retrieval practice that makes memory stick. Keep the intervals roughly as given rather than reviewing everything every day. Check the official page for details on getting started with Anki.

tips: Make cards the same day you learn a topic.
Answer from memory before flipping any card.
Review little and often rather than in one long cram session.

title: Active Recall — The #1 Study Technique You're Not Using

guide.intro: Most students re-read their notes and forget almost everything within a week. Active recall — testing yourself instead of recognising material — builds memory that actually lasts.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Re-reading creates recognition, which feels like learning but fades quickly. Testing yourself forces retrieval, which strengthens the memory. The post cites research by Roediger and Karpicke: students who only re-read remembered around 36 percent a week later, while students who tested themselves remembered around 80 percent.

sections.title: How to use the blank-page trick
sections.text: After each topic, close your notes and write down everything you remember on a blank page. Then open your notes and check the gaps. Those gaps are exactly what you need to study next.

sections.title: What to watch out for
sections.text: Active recall feels harder than re-reading, and that difficulty is the point. Do not judge the method by how easy a session feels. Use it for every subject, not just the ones you find difficult.

tips: Close your notes before you test yourself.
Focus your next review on the gaps you found.
Use self-testing after every topic, not only before exams.
